newsitem.title: GERMANY: Thyssen shares surge on takeover offer.
newsitem.headline: Thyssen shares surge on takeover offer.

text.p: Shares in German steel group Thyssen AG jumped on Tuesday after Fried. Krupp Krupp-Hoesch AG said it would offer 435 marks per Thyssen share.
The shares, which were suspended from regular trade but still changed hands in unofficial trade, leapt to a new high of 410 marks immediately after the news, dealers said.
That was some 65 marks above Thyssen's closing share price in Monday's bourse dealings.
"This is a solid price," said one dealer of the 435 marks per share offer, who forecast an enormous leap to around 400 marks in Thyssen shares once they resumed official trade.
Dealers had predicted an offer price of 430 to 450 marks.
Krupp shares, meanwhile, were trading at about 270 marks, two marks below their last official close on Monday.
Hermann Reith, analyst at BHF Bank in Frankfurt, said the offer by Krupp at first glance was "a bit above expectations".

"But it will be difficult for Thyssen to fight this offer in a short period of time," Reith said. "It will be critical for Thyssen to make its shareholders believe that the company is worth more than this amount."
Reith said he had valued Thyssen shares at about 370 marks on core units and after the divestment of loss-making units.
But Thyssen's participation in the e-plus mobile network adds another 80 marks or so to the share price and real estate reserves add another minimum 20 marks per share.
"The e-plus stake can be sold and the profit potential from core activities is still not proven at the moment. But it will be realised in the next two to three years," Reith said.
Peter Fish, an industry analyst at MEPS in the British steel city Sheffield, called the deal "sort of a reverse takeover".
"I thought it would have been the other way around. But I think it comes together out of necessity."
Rationalisation is needed at both companies and Fish said that could only occur by making bigger units, particularly in Germany.
"The companies have synergies and produce a similar range of products that can molded together to achieve rationalisation particularly within overhead and sales structures."
